text_elements: What this session sets out to achieve, and how success will be measured

To equip learners with a rigorous, modern understanding of K-Means clustering — its Lloyd's-algorithm formulation, and principled techniques (Elbow Method, Silhouette Score) for choosing the number of clusters K.
Introduce K-Means as an unsupervised partitioning method and derive its WCSS objective

Demonstrate the Elbow Method's two-loop structure (outer over K, inner over Lloyd's iterations)
Formalise the Silhouette Score and show how it quantifies cluster cohesion and separation
Guide a hands-on Python walkthrough for each technique using scikit-learn
Explain the K-Means objective function and why Lloyd's Algorithm minimises it monotonically
Implement the Assign and Update steps of Lloyd's Algorithm from first principles
Apply the Elbow Method to select K using WCSS, marginal gain, and curvature
Compute and interpret Silhouette coefficients to validate cluster quality
Compare Elbow vs Silhouette and justify the choice of K for a given dataset

slides.full_text:
K-Means Clustering — Concept
Session 1: Unsupervised partitioning of data into K compact groups
Definition

K-Means partitions a dataset 
X = {x₁,…,xₙ} ⊂ ℝᵈ
 into exactly K non-overlapping clusters C₁,…,Cₖ so that points in the same cluster are as similar as possible, and points in different clusters are as dissimilar as possible.
Unsupervised
No labelled data required
Parametric
User must supply K in advance
Hard assignment
Each point belongs to exactly one cluster
Distance-based
Similarity measured via Euclidean distance
The Postal-Depot Analogy
A courier company places K depots in a city to minimise total parcel travel distance
Each customer address is a data point; each depot is a cluster centroid
Every parcel travels to its nearest depot — this is the hard assignment step
Depots are iteratively relocated to the centre of their assigned customers
Convergence: no parcel benefits from switching, no depot needs to move
Geometric view: K “gravity centres” that alternately attract points and relocate to their centre of mass.

text_elements: The Objective: Within-Cluster Sum of Squares
Session 1: What makes a clustering “good”, mathematically
J = Σₖ₌₁ᵏ Σ ‖xᵢ − μₖ‖²     (sum over xᵢ ∈ Cₖ)
points within a cluster should be close together.
clusters should be far apart from each other.
J sums squared Euclidean distances from every point to its own cluster centroid
Lower J means tighter, more compact clusters — the optimisation target
J = 0 only when every cluster contains a single point (or identical points)
K-Means directly minimises J; it does not explicitly model inter-cluster separation
Elongated or crescent-shaped clusters get split or merged incorrectly
Large clusters dominate; small clusters get absorbed into bigger ones
Dense pockets inside a sparse cluster may form spurious sub-clusters
Categorical or ordinal data needs a different dissimilarity measure

Numerical Example — Silhouette Calculation (Point A)
Validating cluster quality
Step 1
Intra-Cluster
Distance  a(A)
a(A) = (1/3)[d(A,B) + d(A,C) + d(A,D)]
     = (1/3)[1 + 1 + √2]
     = (1/3)(3.414) ≈ 1.138
Step 2
Nearest-Cluster
Distance  b(A)
b(A) = (1/4)[d(A,E)+d(A,F)+d(A,G)+d(A,H)]
     = (1/4)[√98+√113+√113+√128]
     ≈ 10.618
Step 3
Silhouette
Coefficient  s(A)
s(A) = [b(A) − a(A)] / max{a(A), b(A)}
     = (10.618 − 1.138) / 10.618
     ≈  0.893   →  EXCELLENT  ✓
s(A) ≈ 0.893  →  Point A is compactly inside Cluster 1 and well-separated from Cluster 2.  Average s ≈ 0.95  →  Excellent!

text_elements: Session 2: The iterative solver that powers K-Means
Lloyd's Algorithm (1957/1982) is the standard procedure for solving the K-Means objective — an alternating minimisation that provably decreases WCSS at every step until convergence.
Fix centroids; assign each point to its nearest centroid
Each point “magnetises” to whichever centroid is geometrically closest in Euclidean distance.
Fix assignments; recompute each centroid as the mean
μₖ = (1/|Cₖ|) Σ xᵢ   for xᵢ ∈ Cₖ
Each centroid relocates to the centre of mass of its currently-assigned points.
Both steps are individually optimal — Assignment cannot increase WCSS (each point moves to its nearest centroid), and Update cannot increase WCSS (the mean minimises squared deviations).
Since the number of distinct partitions is finite, Lloyd's Algorithm always terminates
slides.full_text:
Lloyd's Algorithm — The Modern View
Session 2: The iterative solver that powers K-Means
Concept:  
Lloyd's Algorithm (1957/1982) is the standard procedure for solving the K-Means objective — an alternating minimisation that provably decreases WCSS at every step until convergence.
STEP 1 — ASSIGNMENT
Fix centroids; assign each point to its nearest centroid
rᵢₖ = 1  if  k = argminₖ′ ‖xᵢ − μₖ′‖²
Each point “magnetises” to whichever centroid is geometrically closest in Euclidean distance.
STEP 2 — UPDATE
Fix assignments; recompute each centroid as the mean
μₖ = (1/|Cₖ|) Σ xᵢ   for xᵢ ∈ Cₖ
Each centroid relocates to the centre of mass of its currently-assigned points.
Convergence Guarantee
Both steps are individually optimal — Assignment cannot increase WCSS (each point moves to its nearest centroid), and Update cannot increase WCSS (the mean minimises squared deviations). 
Since the number of distinct partitions is finite, Lloyd's Algorithm always terminates
, typically in 10–100 iterations in practice.
Session 2 — Lloyd's Algorithm

text_elements: Session 2: Why initialisation matters, and how to do it well
Naive random initialisation can trap Lloyd's Algorithm in a poor local minimum — the algorithm converges, but to a clustering far from optimal.
Choose μ₁ uniformly at random from the dataset X
For k = 2,…,K: choose μₖ with probability proportional to D(x)², where D(x) is the distance to the nearest already-chosen centroid
Points far from existing centroids are far more likely to be picked — this spreads seeds across the data
Run Lloyd's Algorithm to convergence from this initialisation
D(xᵢ) = min over already-chosen centroids μₖ′ of ‖xᵢ − μₖ′‖
Far-away points get higher weight — systematically avoiding clustered, redundant seeds.
Expected WCSS is within O(log K) of the optimal solution — vs O(K) for naive random initialisation.
Always combine k-means++ with multiple restarts (n_init ≥ 10) — scikit-learn's KMeans does this automatically, keeping the run with lowest final WCSS.
slides.full_text:
Smarter Seeding: k-means++
Session 2: Why initialisation matters, and how to do it well
The Problem with Random Seeding
Naive random initialisation can trap Lloyd's Algorithm in a poor local minimum — the algorithm converges, but to a clustering far from optimal.
k-means++ Seeding Procedure
1
Choose μ₁ uniformly at random from the dataset X
2
For k = 2,…,K: choose μₖ with probability proportional to D(x)², where D(x) is the distance to the nearest already-chosen centroid
3
Points far from existing centroids are far more likely to be picked — this spreads seeds across the data
4
Run Lloyd's Algorithm to convergence from this initialisation
Selection Probability
P(xᵢ chosen) = D(xᵢ)² / Σⱼ D(xⱼ)²
D(xᵢ) = min over already-chosen centroids μₖ′ of ‖xᵢ − μₖ′‖
Far-away points get higher weight — systematically avoiding clustered, redundant seeds.
Theoretical Guarantee

Expected WCSS is within O(log K) of the optimal solution — vs O(K) for naive random initialisation.
Practical Tip
Always combine k-means++ with multiple restarts (n_init ≥ 10) — scikit-learn's KMeans does this automatically, keeping the run with lowest final WCSS.

slides.full_text:
Mathematical Foundation of W(K)
Session 3: Defining the inertia curve and its diagnostic quantities
Optimal WCSS at Given K
W(K) = min  Σₖ₌₁ᵏ Σ ‖xᵢ − μₖ‖²
Fundamental Properties
W(K) ≥ 0  for all K
Monotone non-increasing:  W(K+1) ≤ W(K)
W(1) = total variance about the global mean
W(n) = 0   (each point is its own centroid)
Why monotone? 
Any K-cluster partition is also a valid (K+1)-cluster partition (with one empty cluster). So the feasible set only grows — the minimum can only decrease or stay equal.
Three Diagnostic Quantities
Marginal Gain
Δ(K) = W(K−1) − W(K)
How much WCSS improves by adding cluster K
Second Difference (Curvature)
Δ²(K) = W(K−1) − 2W(K) + W(K+1)
Peaks where the curve bends sharpest — the elbow
Elbow Ratio
R(K) = Δ(K) / Δ(K+1)
Always > 1; maximised at the elbow point K*

text_elements: Python in Practice: The Elbow Method
Session 3: scikit-learn implementation, end to end
km.inertia_ returns W(K) directly — scikit-learn already runs k-means++ with multiple restarts internally.
slides.full_text:
Python in Practice: The Elbow Method
Session 3: scikit-learn implementation, end to end
elbow_method.py
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
 
X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=3, random_state=42)
 
wcss = []
K_range = range(1, 11)
for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++',
                n_init=10, random_state=42)
    km.fit(X)
    wcss.append(km.inertia_)   # this is W(K)
 
# Marginal gain and second difference
delta1 = np.diff(wcss)            # Δ(K), sign-flipped
delta2 = np.diff(delta1)          # Δ²(K)
k_star = np.argmax(np.abs(delta2)) + 2
print(f"Suggested K (elbow): {k_star}")
km.inertia_ returns W(K) directly — scikit-learn already runs k-means++ with multiple restarts internally.

Elbow Method — Failure Modes & Checklist
Session 3: Knowing when to trust the elbow, and when not to
Common Failure Modes
No clear elbow
Data lacks compact cluster structure — try Silhouette, DBSCAN, or GMM
Elbow too late
Bad initialisation inflates W(K) at small K — increase n_init; enforce k-means++
Methods disagree
Second-difference is scale-sensitive — trust the visual/kneedle elbow; confirm with Silhouette
Elbow shifts with seed
WCSS estimates are noisy — use ≥ 20 restarts
Unscaled features
WCSS dominated by large-scale features — always z-score standardise first
Step-by-Step Checklist
Scale / standardise all features (z-score)
Choose K_max (typically ≤ √(n/2); start with 10–15)

Silhouette Score — Mathematical Formulation
Session 4: From per-point coefficients to a single quality score
a(i) — Intra-Cluster Distance
a(i) = 1/(|C_z(i)|−1)  Σ d(xᵢ, xⱼ)   for xⱼ ∈ C_z(i), j≠i
Mean distance to every other point in the same cluster
b(i) — Nearest-Cluster Distance
b(i) = minₖ≠z(i)   (1/|Cₖ|) Σ d(xᵢ, xⱼ)   for xⱼ ∈ Cₖ
Mean distance to the closest other cluster (best alternative)
s(i) — Silhouette Coefficient
s(i) = ( b(i) − a(i) ) / max{ a(i), b(i) }    ∈  [−1, +1]
If |C_z(i)| = 1 (singleton cluster), define s(i) = 0
Mean Silhouette Score
s̄ = (1/n) Σᵢ s(i)
Choose  K* = argmaxₖ  s̄

text_elements: Python in Practice: The Silhouette Score

slides.full_text:
Python in Practice: The Silhouette Score
Session 4: scikit-learn implementation, end to end
silhouette_score.py
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
 
X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=3, random_state=42)
 
sil_scores = []
K_range = range(2, 9)        # silhouette needs K ≥ 2
for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++',
                n_init=10, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    score = silhouette_score(X, labels)
    sil_scores.append(score)
 
best_k = list(K_range)[sil_scores.index(max(sil_scores))]
print(f"Best K by Silhouette: {best_k}")
silhouette_samples(X, labels) returns per-point s(i) values — used to draw the silhouette plot.

text_elements: The four ideas to carry forward
Partitions data into K clusters by minimising the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) — a measure of intra-cluster compactness.
Alternates Assign (nearest centroid) and Update (recompute mean) steps; k-means++ seeding and multiple restarts avoid poor local minima.
A two-loop meta-algorithm: outer loop over K, inner loop of Lloyd's iterations. The elbow in the WCSS curve signals diminishing returns.
Per-point coefficient s(i) ∈ [−1,+1] balancing cohesion a(i) and separation b(i); the universal scale makes it the more reliable check.
Together, these three ideas form a complete, principled pipeline: solve for fixed K with Lloyd's Algorithm, then choose K using the Elbow Method and confirm with the Silhouette Score.
